content: The terms woman or mother are used throughout the guideline to refer to individuals who have given birth, regardless of whether they identify as a woman or mother. For simplicity and readability, the term woman is generally used, but mother is sometimes employed when discussing the individual in relation to their newborn. It is acknowledged that some individuals who have given birth may identify as gender-diverse. Additionally, the guideline recognizes the existence of various types of couples and families. The term partner refers to the chosen supporter of the woman, which may include her spouse, partner, or the baby’s father. The term parents encompasses those responsible for the care of the newborn, which may include the mother and father, single parents, co-parents, same-sex parents, or parents with gender-diverse identities. The term caregiver acknowledges the different individuals or family members who may be responsible for the newborn’s care. Families play a critical role in supporting women and parents and are essential to maternal and newborn health. For brevity, these terms are not consistently mentioned throughout the document. The guideline was developed using the standard operating procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The process included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing the evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating of the guideline. The WHO Steering Group supervised the guideline development process. This group included staff from the Departments of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA), Mental Health and Substance Use (MSD), Nutrition and Food Safety (NFS), and Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research (SRH). They drafted the initial scope of the guideline, identified priority questions and outcomes, prepared the guideline planning proposal, and identified systematic review teams, guideline methodologists, and members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The Steering Group also oversaw evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis, organized GDG meetings, prepared draft recommendations, and managed the publication and dissemination of the guideline. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) consisted of 21 external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions. This diverse group included individuals with expertise in research, clinical practice, policy, program development, guideline methodology, and patient/consumer representation. The GDG examined and interpreted evidence, formulated final recommendations, and reviewed and approved the final guideline document. The External Review Group (ERG) included six technical experts and stakeholders with an interest in evidence-based postnatal care. This group peer-reviewed the final document to identify factual errors and provide feedback on language clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. They ensured that the guideline considered the contextual values and preferences of those affected by the recommendations, including postpartum women, partners, newborns, parents, caregivers, families, health workers, and policymakers. The Technical Working Group (TWG) included guideline methodologists and systematic review teams. Independent consultants and technical experts from Centro Rosarino de Estudios Perinatales (CREP) in Argentina served as guideline methodologists. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group (PCG) contributed to the scoping of guideline priority questions and supervised the updating of relevant systematic reviews. Where no suitable systematic reviews existed, new reviews were commissioned by WHO from external experts. The TWG worked closely with the WHO Steering Group to develop or update review protocols, appraise evidence, and prepare GRADE evidence-to-decision frameworks. Representatives from organizations such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), International Pediatric Association (IPA), UNICEF, UNFPA, and USAID were invited to guideline development meetings as observers. These organizations, potential implementers of the guideline, provided comments during technical discussions but did not participate in final recommendation discussions. The WHO Steering Group, in consultation with systematic review teams, guideline methodologists, and selected GDG members, drafted the priority questions for the guideline. Interventions associated with these questions were classified according to the WHO quality of care framework and the nurturing care framework to ensure comprehensive recommendations. The scoping process emphasized the need for person-centered interventions and outcomes for postnatal care. A qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted to understand what women want, need, and value during the postnatal period. This phase is characterized by significant transitions, including changes in self-identity, redefinition of relationships, opportunities for personal growth, and adjustments to sexual behavior, as women adapt to their new roles as parents and individuals within their cultural context. For many women, this period is also marked by feelings of intense joy, happiness, and love for their newborn. The guideline integrates recommendations from existing WHO guidelines relevant to the care of healthy women and babies during the postnatal period. These recommendations, previously approved by the Guideline Review Committee, were incorporated without modification or revalidation, as they were considered current. Some recommendations required adaptation for the purposes of the postnatal care guideline, and relevant WHO departments were consulted to confirm the feasibility of these adaptations. The focus of the guideline is on essential postnatal care, which all women, adolescents, and their newborns should receive to ensure a positive postnatal experience. The GRADE evidence-to-decision framework tool was used to synthesize and examine evidence across relevant domains, including benefits, harms, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility of each intervention. Evidence on maternal clinical practices was primarily derived from Cochrane systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials. Where Cochrane reviews were outdated, authors were invited to update their reviews. New systematic reviews were commissioned where necessary, with protocols reviewed and approved by the WHO Steering Group. Qualitative reviews were also commissioned to explore women’s and health workers’ perspectives on postnatal care, including discharge preparation and readiness from health facilities after birth.
